messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Violence: Violence, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Nadia Hassan is a 52-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who works as a project manager for a large commercial construction firm. She is married and had long thought of herself as practical, sociable, and steady under pressure, the kind of person who could keep a timeline moving and reassure everyone else when problems came up. The event that now divides her life into a before and after happened eighteen months ago, during a work trip downtown for a meeting with contractors and city officials. She had just stepped out onto a crowded street near a municipal building when an explosion tore through the block ahead. The force of it threw people to the ground. Glass shattered outward. In the first seconds she did not understand what had happened, only that there was screaming, smoke, and the sight of people running in every direction. Then came the sound that she still cannot describe without tensing in her chair: sirens closing in, police shouting commands, and helicopters circling so low overhead that she could feel the vibration in her chest. She remembers seeing armed officers push through the crowd while injured people lay on the pavement and bystanders cried out for help. What remains most vivid to her is not a complete narrative but those fragments—the violence in front of her, the commands from police, the aircraft overhead—fixed in a way that still feels immediate.

In the weeks afterward, Nadia returned home physically unharmed, but she felt as if something essential had been altered. She would tell her husband that she used to be a happy person, someone who laughed easily and looked forward to dinners with friends, and that now she woke with a heaviness she could not shake. She was troubled by how unfamiliar she felt to herself. Sitting in her kitchen in the morning, dressed for work and staring at her coffee, she would think, I don’t know who I am anymore. The change felt visible to her, almost stamped onto her face. When she entered meetings, she had the uneasy conviction that other people could tell what had happened to her just by looking at her, as though the event had marked her in some obvious way. Even when colleagues said nothing unusual, she found herself searching their expressions for signs that they had noticed her.

Because her job keeps her in constant contact with city sites, contractors, and public agencies, reminders began appearing in ordinary parts of the day. On one project, police officers were stationed outside a government-adjacent building, and the sight of their uniforms and authoritative posture made her body go rigid before she had time to think. She would lower her eyes, hurry past, and later replay the moment with embarrassment, certain she had looked strange. At construction sites, the sudden chop of a helicopter overhead could pull her out of a conversation mid-sentence. The noise did not register to her as neutral background sound; it landed with the same sense of alarm as the day of the bombing, and she would stop talking until it passed. News clips or even overheard talk about assaults, shootings, or other acts of violence had a similar effect. She would turn off the television, leave the room, or ask her husband not to tell her details, because violent scenes felt too close to what she had witnessed on the street.

Over the following months, these adjustments narrowed her life. She began asking subordinates to attend site visits that involved municipal buildings or downtown security perimeters. She chose remote meetings when she could and reorganized project schedules to avoid being physically present in places where police presence was likely. At work, this made her feel less competent and less like the leader she had been. A few colleagues noticed that she was delegating field responsibilities she once handled herself, and although no one confronted her directly, Nadia was convinced they could see her change. At home she became quieter. Her husband would suggest visiting family friends or going into the city for dinner, and she would decline, saying she was tired. What pained her most was not only the misery itself but the conviction that the person her husband married had somehow disappeared.

By the time she sought help, the immediate anniversary of the attack had passed, but the sense of living under its shadow had not. The final push came after she was walking from a client meeting and heard a helicopter overhead while police vehicles blocked part of the street for an unrelated incident. She froze on the sidewalk, unable for several moments to continue, and afterward sat in her car shaken and ashamed. She told herself that this was no way to keep living or working. In coming to treatment, Nadia says she wants some way to feel recognizable to herself again. What frightens her most is the idea that this miserable, exposed version of her is now permanent, that she will never again move through the world without feeling that the violence is still close and that everyone around her can see it.
